data.title: Nevus depigmentosus — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus depigmentosus** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is nevus depigmentosus (achromic naevus)?**
- Congenital, stable, well-circumscribed hypopigmented (not depigmented) macule or patch with irregular serrated ('splashed paint') border; present at birth or noticed in early childhood (by age 3) as pigmentation of surrounding skin increases; grows in proportion with the child
- Mosaic disorder of melanosome transfer — normal or slightly reduced melanocyte number with reduced melanin synthesis/transfer

**Q2. Clinical types.**
- Isolated (single round/oval or irregular patch — commonest on trunk, proximal limbs)
- Segmental (band-like along a dermatome-like/Blaschkoid segment, does not cross midline)
- Systematised (whorled/streaky along Blaschko's lines — overlaps hypomelanosis of Ito; check for neurological, ocular, skeletal anomalies)

**Q3. How do you differentiate it from vitiligo and nevus anaemicus?**
- Vitiligo: acquired, chalk-white (depigmented), bright Wood's lamp fluorescence, sharp convex borders, progressive, leucotrichia, absent melanocytes
- Nevus depigmentosus: congenital/stable, off-white (hypopigmented), Wood's lamp — off-white without bright fluorescence, serrated border, normal hairs, melanocytes present
- Nevus anaemicus: pharmacological vasoconstriction (increased α-adrenergic sensitivity); pale patch disappears on diascopy (blends with blanched surrounding skin) and does not redden on rubbing; normal Wood's lamp

**Q4. Other differentials.**
- Ash-leaf macules (tuberous sclerosis — multiple, look for other signs), piebaldism, pityriasis alba, indeterminate leprosy (sensation), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, segmental vitiligo, hypopigmented MF, tinea versicolor

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Clinical with Wood's lamp, dermoscopy; biopsy rarely — normal/slightly reduced melanocytes with reduced melanin (Fontana–Masson), abnormal melanosome aggregates in melanocytes on EM
- Screen for systemic features in systematised type; check sensation to exclude leprosy

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance; cosmetic camouflage
- Phototherapy poorly effective; surgical options — suction blister grafting, non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (melanocyte–keratinocyte transplant) give good results due to stability; excimer laser in some

**Q7. What is the histopathology in detail?**
- Normal epidermis with reduced melanin on Fontana–Masson; melanocyte number normal or slightly reduced (S100/ Melan-A); EM — normal melanosomes aggregated within melanocytes, reduced transfer to keratinocytes

**Q8. What is the association with systemic anomalies?**
- Usually isolated; systematised type may overlap with hypomelanosis of Ito and rarely shows neurological/ musculoskeletal/ ocular associations — examine and refer as needed

**Q9. What surgical options and outcomes?**
- Stability makes surgical repigmentation suitable: suction blister epidermal grafts, mini-punch grafts, non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (MKTP) — reported good repigmentation, though perifollicular/ marginal hypopigmentation may persist; excimer/ NB-UVB adjunct

**Q10. Differentiate ND from ash-leaf macule.**
- Ash-leaf macules: multiple (≥3), lance-ovate, from birth, with other TSC signs (angiofibromas, shagreen patch, seizures) — Wood's lamp highlights; ND usually single, irregular serrated margin, no systemic features

**Q11. Differentiate ND from nevus anaemicus at bedside.**
- Diascopy: nevus anaemicus disappears (blends with blanched surrounding skin), ND remains
- Rubbing/ heat: nevus anaemicus does not become erythematous (vasoconstriction), ND shows normal erythema
- Wood's lamp: nevus anaemicus not accentuated; ND shows off-white accentuation

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. Describe the pathogenesis.**
- Functional defect of melanocytes in a mosaic clone — reduced melanosome production and defective transfer to keratinocytes (aggregated melanosomes within melanocytes on EM); melanocyte number normal or slightly reduced

**Q14. Diagnostic criteria (Coupe's criteria).**
- Leucoderma present at birth or early in life; no alteration in distribution throughout life; no alteration in texture or sensation of the affected area; no hyperpigmented border

**Q15. Dermoscopy of nevus depigmentosus vs vitiligo.**
- ND: faint, reduced pigment network with irregular/serrated edges and preserved perifollicular pigment, no leucotrichia; vitiligo: absent network, perifollicular pigmentation (repigmenting), white glow, leucotrichia, trichrome/ starburst pattern in active disease

## Quick spotter facts
- Stable congenital off-white patch with serrated border, Wood's lamp not bright — nevus depigmentosus
- Nevus anaemicus disappears on diascopy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
